articles.content: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) recently rejected the collective shunning of Russian athletes in international hockey. In doing so, it created a geopolitical test of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s key foreign policy tenets. The current exclusion of Russian teams stems from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), along with the International Olympic Committee and FIFA, banned Russia and its ally, Belarus, from their competitions as part of the wider global effort to penalize the Kremlin. The IIHF reiterated its position in early 2026, citing the safety and security of all participants and the “ integrity of its competitions .” In October, a three-member CAS tribunal found that unconvincing: there was insufficient evidence to establish the legal requirements for non-participation. Only substantiated security concerns could justify national exclusions. The CAS set aside the IIHF decision on procedural grounds and left it at that. Naturally, the Russian Ice Hockey Federation welcomed the decision and declared its intention to participate in the World Junior Championship in Alberta starting on Dec. 26. Banned by Canada Hockey federations in Canada and Europe expressed varying degrees of disappointment , with some countries threatening to boycott games against Russian players. Germany is threatening to abdicate its hosting duties for the May 2027 Men’s World Championship if Russia participates. Carney called the return of Russian teams “ unwelcome ” and later said the the Russian team would be barred from competing in Alberta for the World Juniors . The IIHF has since made Russia’s exclusion from the December-January World Juniors complete by yielding to the Canadian government’s restrictions. Russian officials were apoplectic and the IIHF website was hit by cyber attacks . Notably, USA Hockey has been quiet. CAS decision and Canadian foreign policy The CAS ruling and its fallout may be peripheral to what is known as great power politics , but it’s also a test of the post-rules-based global order. For Canada, the implications of disregarding the CAS ruling are considerable. For decades, Canada’s foreign policy was premised on the legitimacy of international institutions and a commitment to multilateralism . The CAS is one component of the interlocking machinery of that order. Now, major hockey countries like Canada find themselves on the horns of a dilemma: accept the CAS ruling and undermine the collective pressure campaign against Russia, or ignore the ruling and accelerate the erosion of yet another multilateral institution. Two or three years ago, Canada might have held its nose and accepted the CAS decision because of its procedural legitimacy. Trusting the global process was Canada’s overall strategy for decades but under Carney, that’s no longer the case. Yet, even in this period of “rupture ,” multilateral rules are still important. It’s not clear there’s any more wisdom in accelerating the old order’s demise than there is in practising what Carney has called “ naïve multilateralism .” Read more: Mark Carney’s Davos speech marks a major departure from Canada’s usual approach to the U.S. Canada’s bad options As host of the World Juniors, Canada was the first country with a decision to make — and future hosts are watching. Allowing the Russians to participate was likely never going to happen. Unfortunately, every option comes at a high cost. The easiest approach would have been to say it was too late to include Russia in the 2026 World Juniors. That would have eased pressure on the federal government and Hockey Canada, but it would have passed the buck to the Czech Republic, hosts of the Under-18 Women’s World Championship in January 2027 . It also wouldn’t have been the type of middle power leadership that Canada has been trying to signal. Another half-measure would have been to allow Russia’s players to compete under a neutral banner , but that doesn’t fool anyone and has even been used by Russia’s propagandists as a point of pride . The option Canada ultimately took is, ironically, right out of Donald Trump’s playbook: ignore the CAS decision and make up your own rules. Carney’s declaration that “Russians will not be there” means denying entry visas to players, coaches and staff, much like what the American president did to Iran prior to the 2026 FIFA World Cup. For Canada though, ignoring inconvenient rulings is vice masquerading as virtue. Back in from the cold? Regardless of Canada’s decision, the integration of Russia into the sporting fold is already underway in both the IOC and FIFA. The Court of Arbitration’s decision may serve as the basis for further reintegration — and Trump may accelerate the process. He’ll still be president when the United States hosts the Men’s Under-18 Hockey World Championship in April 2027 and the Summer Olympic Games in 2028. Trump’s pro-Russia tendencies may prompt him to strongarm the IIHF and IOC into bringing Russia back in from the cold. For now, the Carney government has leaned into the rupture. Ignoring the court ruling, blocking Russia’s participation and standing with Canada’s European allies is consistent with Carney’s new skepticism toward the aforementioned naive multilateralism. But it comes at a cost to whatever remains of the rules-based international order . articles.content: Carrie-Anne Moss in Crave's _YAGA_. The series, based on the play of the same name, draws on Baba Yaga from East European folklore. (Crave/Christopher Lawrence) Baba Yaga is a terrifying witch from eastern European folklore , found in folktales from Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and other Slavic countries. Yet she is more than just a scary monster. In many folktales, she offers advice and assistance to characters who are kind and clever, while punishing rude, selfish ones. Baba Yaga’s intriguing duality — her ability to be both a villain and a saviour, a figure of destruction and renewal, of darkness and light — has inspired artists and writers to produce lively adaptations that have travelled well beyond eastern European folklore and made her a favourite among audiences worldwide. The recent Crave series YAGA , starring Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams, is the latest in a long history of versions of her tales . The series, whose showrunner wrote the acclaimed play of the same name , imagines “ the myth of Baba Yaga as a contemporary mystery thriller .” As an anthropologist who has studied folklore and witchcraft, I want to examine the original Baba Yaga and how she has been received by western audiences. Trailer for ‘Yaga,’ starring Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams. Deep in a forest In folktales, Baba Yaga lives deep in the forest in a round house that spins on chicken feet, surrounded by a fence made from the bones and skulls of her victims — a grim warning of her cannibalistic nature to anyone who would dare intrude on her. She flies through the skies in a giant mortar and pestle, making a dreadful noise as she crushes her victim’s bones. Baba Yaga takes her place alongside similar villainous folktale witches; in Slavic folktales, she plays the role of the witches in tales like Hansel and Gretel, Snow White and Sleeping Beauty, whose purpose is often to both frighten and test the folktale protagonist. At the same time, her unique characteristics make her a classic figure of eastern European folklore who has become a symbol of Russian cultural identity . Beyond being a villainous witch, she can also help a sympathetic character find their missing family member, provide wealth and prosperity and even reveal the secrets of immortality. Her actions reward the kinds of behaviours that are helpful in human societies while punishing those that violate popular morality, emphasizing values that are important to storytellers and their audiences. ‘Russian Folktales’ of 1863 Oral tales of Baba Yaga date back to the days of the ancient Rus’, the ancestors of modern Russians . She first came to the attention of western readers through Alexander Afanasyev’s massive collection, Russian Folktales , published between 1855 and 1863. Almost all later adaptations of Baba Yaga stories are based on tales from this collection. Her popularity in the West increased after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. There have now been countless book and dramatic adaptations featuring Baba Yaga. Like other folkloric witches, Baba Yaga has been interpreted through a variety of lenses, each offering a perspective on why she continues to fascinate us. Russian structuralist Vladimir Propp argued that the folktale hero’s quest can be read as an initiation rite into self-knowledge and adulthood . ‘Grandmother Yaga’ Baba Yaga, whose name means “grandmother Yaga,” acts as both a challenger and a maternal figure who ushers the hero or heroine into the world of adulthood. The protagonist journeys into the dark forest where they encounter Baba Yaga, who tests their courage and wisdom by assigning impossible tasks, asking difficult questions or presenting opportunities for heroes and heroines to show their mettle. She rewards strength, courage, cleverness and facing up to her challenges, giving protagonists the ability to return home and thrive in everyday life. The protagonists come back forever changed, having gained both self-knowledge and wisdom, the very qualities that define maturity. Insights from psychology A number of scholars have offered psychological interpretations of Baba Yaga, ranging from strictly Freudian to more nuanced perspectives . Psychologist Bruno Bettelheim, who wrote about the meaning of fairy tales in his book The Uses of Enchantment , emphasized how Baba Yaga’s dual nature reflects a child’s view of its mother as a source of both love and nurture, and fear of punishment . But the fairy-tale witch might have different meanings for children of different ages. For very small children, Baba Yaga may primarily be a scary figure meant to frighten them into compliance with adult wishes. For older children, she can represent the often hostile but sometimes helpful strangers who usher them into a world of greater responsibility and self-confidence. Detail of Baba Yaga from a larger watercolour illustrating Russian fairy tale Maria Morevna. (Giles Watson/Flickr) , CC BY-SA Feminist interpretations Early feminist interpretations drew parallels between Baba Yaga and the Great Mother goddess, a feminine deity of fertility, death and regeneration alleged to have been worshipped by some prehistoric European cultures . More recent feminist interpretations focus on the witch as embodying the shadow side of the female in male-dominated societies: the woman who cannot or will not be dominated . As the opposite of what patriarchal society expects of women, she is monstrous, aggressive and frightening: she destroys men and eats children, the reverse of the alluring seductress and nurturing mother. Yet the witch is powerful exactly because she exists without the permission or control of men. Baba Yaga lives by herself deep in the forest, the heart of the natural world; she alone controls who can cross her bony fence. In a post #MeToo era in which women’s rights to bodily autonomy are once again under attack, she has become a symbol of resistance against male dominance, violence against women and environmental destruction . articles.content: “The only way we’re gonna get through this,” Lucia tells Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6), “is by sticking together.” GTA6 is, unlike its predecessors, built around a relationship between two lead characters. The game tracks their level of intimacy on a four-point scale : running on empty , partners in crime , crazy in love and hot together . As a player, you must actively maintain the bond between them — by having them be nice to each other, go on dates and of course work together to commit crimes. And yes, they even have sex. The game has a relationship meter that allows players to watch the connection between the two rise and fall. Rob Nelson, Rockstar North’s head of development, told The Verge : “You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.” For some people, this idea, that a video game is trying to simulate a normal human relationship, will immediately set off alarm bells about the dangers of digital intimacy, especially for teenagers. I don’t think there is much to worry about. GTA6 is an immersive experience, to be sure, and players are definitely going to become invested in Lucia and Jason’s romance. But their interactions are scripted. Will artificial intimacy diminish us? Recently we have heard lots of dire warnings about what MIT researcher Sherry Turkle calls “artificial intimacy.” Turkle has recently published a book warning about the risks of emotional connections with artificial entities . In it, she says: “If these are the relationships we choose, we will be left in a world of non-relationships. Artificial intimacy is positioned to colonize and diminish the human kind.” Governments are also increasingly concerned about the risks of AI companionship, particularly for minors. China has prohibited AI companions for underage users. In the United States, several states have passed laws restricting or banning AI companions. U.S. congress is considering a federal law that would prohibit minors from using them. Tens of millions of people, including, inevitably, many teenagers, will play GTA6 in the coming months, and will experience first-hand the artificial intimacy between Jason and Lucia. They will spend hours deliberately fostering and building that intimacy. Should we be worried? A game that encourages empathy Turkle is mostly concerned about AI companions that engage users in open-ended conversations and respond directly to their emotional needs. These bots can create the impression of a reciprocal relationship with a partner who is responsive and emotionally invested. That’s a very different experience from developing a relationship between two fictional characters within a game. Also, GTA6 offers a notably positive vision of romance. Turkle argues that digital technologies allow us to experience the comforts of companionship without having to face up to the demands of human relationships. She argues that artificial intimacy is too easy, and this turns us off the messiness that comes with real attachment. GTA6 models something different. Jason and Lucia have to nurture their bond. They must talk to each other and be attentive to each other’s needs. Lucia reminds Jason: “Relationships are about communication, Jay.” And because players can switch between characters, they experience the relationship from both sides. As Rob Nelson, one of the three creative leads on GTA6 at Rockstar North, told The Guardian : “We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage empathy — for those who want it.” Arguably, Lucia and Jason show us just the sort of relationship that Turkle believes is threatened by technology. A transactional logic Though we definitely shouldn’t panic about GTA6’s digital intimacy, I do think there are aspects of the relationship that are worth noticing. The game is built around optimization. Players raise the couple’s bond meter through specific actions and the rewards are concrete. As the meter rises, the couple holds hands and kisses. At the top tier, the game unlocks the option for sex. Affection is a score, and intimacy becomes something the player earns by supplying the right inputs. Once the meter is maxed out, the couple never fights. In this way, it reproduces the sort of transactional logic that worries many critics of AI companions. In the game, these things are pretty harmless. The relationship is between two fictional characters, rather than between a user and a machine that claims to care about them. And no one profits from how attached the player becomes to Lucia or Jason. But the dynamic parallels some of the ways AI companion apps operate, and these can be more insidious. With these apps, the equivalent mechanics — reminders that your companion misses you, intimate content that is unlocked through engagement or by paying — are central to the business model. The laws of virtual romance As we debate whether and how to regulate AI companionship, the lesson here is not to target an entire class of technology. Blanket bans on AI companions are not the answer. Artificial intimacy can be harmless, or even positive, for users . Rather, we should focus on specific design features that can cause harm, particularly to young people. We should, for instance, look at the way AI companion apps are designed to maximize engagement, the way they use emotional pressure as a retention tactic and the way they present affection and sex as a reward for specific behaviours. Jason and Lucia are poised to become the digital world’s two most famous outlaws. It would be a nice irony if they end up teaching us a lesson about how to write better laws governing virtual romance. The game tracks their level of intimacy on a four-point scale : running on empty , partners in crime , crazy in love and hot together . As a player, you must actively maintain the bond between them — by having them be nice to each other, go on dates and of course work together to commit crimes. And yes, they even have sex. The game has a relationship meter that allows players to watch the connection between the two rise and fall. Rob Nelson, Rockstar North’s head of development, told The Verge : “You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.” For some people, this idea, that a video game is trying to simulate a normal human relationship, will immediately set off alarm bells about the dangers of digital intimacy, especially for teenagers. I don’t think there is much to worry about. GTA6 is an immersive experience, to be sure, and players are definitely going to become invested in Lucia and Jason’s romance. But their interactions are scripted. Will artificial intimacy diminish us? Recently we have heard lots of dire warnings about what MIT researcher Sherry Turkle calls “artificial intimacy.” Turkle has recently published a book warning about the risks of emotional connections with artificial entities . In it, she says: “If these are the relationships we choose, we will be left in a world of non-relationships. Artificial intimacy is positioned to colonize and diminish the human kind.” Governments are also increasingly concerned about the risks of AI companionship, particularly for minors. China has prohibited AI companions for underage users. In the United States, several states have passed laws restricting or banning AI companions. U.S. congress is considering a federal law that would prohibit minors from using them. Tens of millions of people, including, inevitably, many teenagers, will play GTA6 in the coming months, and will experience first-hand the artificial intimacy between Jason and Lucia. They will spend hours deliberately fostering and building that intimacy. Should we be worried? A game that encourages empathy Turkle is mostly concerned about AI companions that engage users in open-ended conversations and respond directly to their emotional needs. These bots can create the impression of a reciprocal relationship with a partner who is responsive and emotionally invested. That’s a very different experience from developing a relationship between two fictional characters within a game. Also, GTA6 offers a notably positive vision of romance. Turkle argues that digital technologies allow us to experience the comforts of companionship without having to face up to the demands of human relationships. She argues that artificial intimacy is too easy, and this turns us off the messiness that comes with real attachment. GTA6 models something different. Jason and Lucia have to nurture their bond. They must talk to each other and be attentive to each other’s needs. Lucia reminds Jason: “Relationships are about communication, Jay.” And because players can switch between characters, they experience the relationship from both sides. As Rob Nelson, one of the three creative leads on GTA6 at Rockstar North, told The Guardian : “We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage empathy — for those who want it.” Arguably, Lucia and Jason show us just the sort of relationship that Turkle believes is threatened by technology. A transactional logic Though we definitely shouldn’t panic about GTA6’s digital intimacy, I do think there are aspects of the relationship that are worth noticing. The game is built around optimization. Players raise the couple’s bond meter through specific actions and the rewards are concrete. As the meter rises, the couple holds hands and kisses. At the top tier, the game unlocks the option for sex. Affection is a score, and intimacy becomes something the player earns by supplying the right inputs. Once the meter is maxed out, the couple never fights. In this way, it reproduces the sort of transactional logic that worries many critics of AI companions. In the game, these things are pretty harmless. The relationship is between two fictional characters, rather than between a user and a machine that claims to care about them. And no one profits from how attached the player becomes to Lucia or Jason. But the dynamic parallels some of the ways AI companion apps operate, and these can be more insidious. With these apps, the equivalent mechanics — reminders that your companion misses you, intimate content that is unlocked through engagement or by paying — are central to the business model. The laws of virtual romance As we debate whether and how to regulate AI companionship, the lesson here is not to target an entire class of technology. Blanket bans on AI companions are not the answer. Artificial intimacy can be harmless, or even positive, for users . Rather, we should focus on specific design features that can cause harm, particularly to young people. We should, for instance, look at the way AI companion apps are designed to maximize engagement, the way they use emotional pressure as a retention tactic and the way they present affection and sex as a reward for specific behaviours. Jason and Lucia are poised to become the digital world’s two most famous outlaws. It would be a nice irony if they end up teaching us a lesson about how to write better laws governing virtual romance. articles.content: For post-secondary students, every new academic year inevitably comes with tuition bills, textbook costs and a long list of student fees, as well as mandatory health plans . Students are locked into a number of plans covering outpatient prescription drugs, dental, extended health and virtual health care, but they’re not allowed to opt out of their school plans without comparable private insurance. These plans make Ontario college and university students under age 25 ineligible for the Ontario Health Insurance Plan Plus (OHIP+) , which covers nearly 6,000 medications at no out-of-pocket cost. Ontario’s Liberal government introduced OHIP+ in January 2018, providing free prescription drug coverage to eligible residents under 25, regardless of private insurance. In April 2019, Premier Doug Ford’s Conservative government restricted OHIP+ to cover only those who did not otherwise have private coverage . As OHIP coverage cannot be used to opt out of school plans, thousands of post-secondary students lost access to Ontario’s public drug program. To examine how Ontario post-secondary students may have been affected by this sudden change, we reviewed prescription drug plans across colleges and universities. We documented all cost-sharing components (for example, deductible, co-insurance, co-payment, dispensing fees and annual limits), specific coverage for contraceptives and exclusions . We then compared students’ coverage to the coverage available under OHIP. Variations in plans We identified substantial variation in prescription drug coverage across university and college student health plans, resulting in important inequities. There were significant disparities in cost-sharing and contraceptive coverage. Students were responsible for paying anywhere from zero per cent to 50 per cent of their prescription costs, most commonly 20 per cent. Annual coverage limits ranged from $250 to $12,500. Additionally, colleges in northern Ontario generally offered less comprehensive coverage and imposed more restrictive reimbursement criteria. Notably, none of the plans sponsored by student unions compared favourably with coverage available through OHIP. Contraceptive coverage varied considerably across institutions. Some plans covered oral contraceptives but excluded other methods such as devices and implants. Others imposed product-specific reimbursement limits, while some provided no contraceptive coverage at all. These gaps are especially concerning given that the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada identifies intrauterine devices as a first-line contraceptive option for adolescents and young adults. This illustrates the disconnect between evidence-based clinical guidelines and private insurance coverage policies. Many coverage restrictions affect conditions that already carry significant stigma, particularly among young adults. Treatments for smoking cessation, obesity, acne, infertility and erectile dysfunction were frequently excluded from coverage, subject to reimbursement caps or otherwise restricted. Such limitations may create additional barriers to care, as students may be reluctant to seek treatment because of financial concerns, stigma or both. Smoking cessation therapies were frequently excluded from student health plan coverage. In contrast, OHIP provides coverage for prescription smoking cessation medications for individuals aged 18 years and older, as well as up to one year of pharmacist-led smoking cessation counselling. In 2020, the United States Surgeon General highlighted the critical role of insurance coverage in supporting smoking cessation, stating: “Insurance coverage for smoking cessation treatment that is comprehensive, barrier-free, and widely promoted increases the use of these treatment services, leads to higher rates of successful quitting, and is cost-effective.” Impact on health and access to care Higher prescription drug costs can have important consequences for students’ health and access to care. Research from Canada and internationally consistently shows that people are more likely to use medications when they have insurance and face lower out-of-pocket costs. Conversely, losing insurance or facing higher costs can reduce medication use. A recent study in JAMA Pediatrics found that the introduction of universal coverage in Ontario in 2018 led to increases in contraceptive dispensations and decreases after restrictions were introduced. Beyond the equity and health implications of the April 2019 changes to Ontario’s public drug program, important efficiency concerns also arise. Public drug insurance programs such as OHIP are generally more efficient than private insurance mechanisms, including post-secondary student plans, in collecting revenue, sharing financial risk and administering coverage. As a result, public systems can often deliver comparable or more comprehensive coverage at a lower overall cost than fragmented private insurance arrangements. The modest reductions in government spending associated with the 2019 cuts are unlikely to offset the additional costs imposed on Ontario residents. Given the inherent and increasing inefficiencies of private insurance, including higher administrative expenses and less effective risk pooling , shifting coverage from the public to the private sector is likely to increase overall system costs and lead to higher premiums for students and their families. articles.content: How much public support does a company need before it can build a major development in a community? And who gets to decide if that threshold is met? These questions are emerging in New Brunswick, where two communities are approaching the prospect of AI data centre development differently. In Fundy Shores, the mayor has called for new rules governing AI data centres , even though no developer has proposed building one in his municipality yet. The municipality wants future data centre developers to obtain council approval through a rezoning process, giving residents an opportunity to weigh in before construction could proceed. In nearby Saint John, residents have been debating a proposed facility in Lorneville . At a public meeting, they raised concerns about air quality, water consumption and the benefits such a project would bring. After the meeting, one resident told reporters: “I think it demonstrates that there is no social licence for this project.” The two communities illustrate different points in the debate over social license: how to establish public support for a project before it is proposed, and what happens when residents believe that support is absent. As an environmental communication researcher, I have studied how supporters and opponents of liquefied natural gas development in British Columbia made competing claims about whose interests those projects would serve. I see similar disputes in debates over AI data centres, particularly when different parties claim to speak for the people who will live alongside a project. What is a social licence? Having a “social licence to operate” refers to the ongoing acceptance of a project by people affected by it . The term emerged in the mining industry in the 1990s, when companies recognized that even with government permits in hand, opposition from neighbours could delay or disrupt their operations. It captured the practical importance of public support, though it left open who could grant it or judge when it had been lost. Unlike a government permit, a social licence is not a formal legal authorization. It’s an informal relationship between a developer and the communities affected by its activities. Consider the debate over Enbridge’s proposed Northern Gateway pipeline . In April 2014, residents of Kitimat, B.C., where the pipeline was proposed to terminate, voted on the project. Of those who voted, 58.4 per cent opposed it . Read more: Where does all the hardware go? The hidden environmental footprint of AI data centres What followed was a political dispute about how much weight residents’ responses should carry . Opponents pointed to that result as evidence that Enbridge had failed to earn local acceptance. An idea the mining industry had used to explain why companies needed public support had given residents a way to express their opposition. Some pipeline advocates, including newspaper columnists and Conservative politicians, objected that opponents were claiming a veto over projects of national importance. A company could welcome consultation, yet disagree about what should happen when residents rejected its proposal. Whose support counts? Claims that a project has or lacks a social licence often depend on who is speaking for the community, and whose views are being counted. The public meeting in Saint John gave some residents a chance to voice their concerns, but it could not establish how the wider community felt about the proposal. The same challenge arises when projects are presented as having public support. A council resolution reflects elected representatives’ positions; a benefits agreement records what its signatories accepted while a public vote reflects the views of those who participated. Each provides evidence about a different group of people , but none necessarily represents everyone affected. This question of representation is especially important when projects affect Indigenous nations. First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities have distinct rights, governing institutions and authority to make decisions. Their views cannot be subsumed into municipal consultation or treated as another measure of local opinion. What if a community changes its mind? There is a danger to treating social licence as a one-time decision, as I mentioned in a recent interview about Fundy Shores . Before a data centre is constructed, residents have forecasts and promises to consider. Once a facility opens, they can measure those promises against their lived experiences, including how the operator responds when something goes wrong. Sherbrooke, Que., offers one example of how the experience of a project after it opens can change how a community views it. The city agreed to supply electricity to Bitfarms for a bitcoin mining facility . Soon after it opened, neighbours began complaining to the city about the noise. Bitfarms replaced the fans and installed a noise barrier, but the problem persisted. In 2021, the city and the company agreed in principle to move the operation to an industrial park . A social licence, then, is not something a developer keeps indefinitely. It largely depends on whether a project continues to meet the expectations of the people affected by it. Residents views may change as a project develops and its impacts become clearer. A council’s approval may allow construction to proceed, but it does not guarantee lasting community acceptance. Residents must have opportunities to hold operators accountable as they experience the project’s effects. articles.content: Climate activists at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey , awarded Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney a Fossil of the Day award , along with other leaders from wealthy countries who skipped the summit. The satirical award is given to countries and leaders seen as doing little to support efforts to tackle climate change. The award was not the only criticism of Carney’s climate credentials. Newsweek listed the prime minister at No. 2 on a list of “climate heretics,” just behind Microsoft founder Bill Gates and ahead of United States President Donald Trump. These criticisms might seem surprising, as Carney has been seen as a climate champion. At the 2015 COP in Paris , Carney said companies need to develop plans for net-zero emissions . Yet, after becoming prime minister, he scrapped the federal consumer carbon tax and signed an agreement with Alberta to push forward a new oil pipeline. How should we make sense of the Fossil of the Day award? How did Carney go from seeming climate hero to climate villain? As sociologists, we have written about and researched environmental activism around COP summits. These gatherings are not only places for policy discussions. They provide a platform for activists to push for action and direct criticism toward obstructive governments and corporations. Fossil of the Day as a strategic event Social movements take advantage of global events such as COP to name and shame political leaders or corporations that they identify as climate villains . At COP summits, the Climate Action Network hosts the Fossil of the Day award, as well as some other awards. The ceremony resembles a TV comedy sketch, where activists describe the key climate negotiation events they wish to highlight, and set out to embarrass those obstructing progress. While this is going on, a person in a dinosaur suit dances and music from Jurassic Park plays. Meanwhile, activists sing songs with lyrics they make up for the event. Fossil of the Day is about taking advantage of a critical event. Groups like the Climate Action Network award Fossils of the Day to try to affect media coverage, influence public opinion and ultimately pressure governments to take greater action to tackle climate change. Some critical events like COP happen on a regular schedule that is known in advance. We have referred to these as regularly scheduled critical events . Groups can plan ahead and take advantage of opportunities to comment on and critique the conversations going on in official spaces of deliberation among global leaders. Relatedly, interaction ritual theory explains phenomena that often occur in the context of a common action or event . Some key elements of the process include: group assembly (bodily co-presence), mutual focus of attention and shared mood. Engagement in interaction rituals often fosters group solidarity, emotional energy, symbols of social relationship and standards of morality. We can think about the Fossil of the Day in these terms. Activists and other COP participants routinely try to attend the Fossil of the Day award. It is an opportunity to meet up and rub elbows. Participants benefit from camaraderie, some light-hearted humour, and also, in some cases, righteous anger directed at leaders, governments and other bodies who obstruct climate action. These get-togethers reinforce social ties among the participants. Canada: Climate hero to climate villain? At COP21 in Paris, then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau announced, “Canada is back!” The Trudeau government’s environment minister, Catherine McKenna, helped to negotiate the Paris Climate Agreement . One of Carney’s first acts as prime minister was to cancel the consumer carbon tax Trudeau brought in. And, among other things, Carney is now working to develop new oil and gas projects . At COP31, Carney was a no-show at the leaders summit. This past week, two former environment and climate change ministers criticized the record and direction of the current government. McKenna stated that the claim that Canada is still committed to its targets is “factually untrue.” Indeed, Canada consistently has one of the worst climate performance records . The Climate Change Performance Index, which compares the climate performance of 64 countries and the European Union, ranks Canada 62nd . This poor performance started before Carney’s tenure as prime minister , but Canada has been backsliding on the climate change file since he took office. In the view of many Canadians, Canada faces serious, and even existential, threats from the Trump-led United States. In the wake of this threat, Carney has been trying to boost economic growth and diversify international and domestic trade. Much of this has involved plans to grow the fossil fuel sector . The strategy has also been an attempt to assuage discontent fuelling separatist sentiments in oil-rich Alberta. What is not entirely clear is whether the direction of Carney’s energy and climate policies is a short-term strategy to deal with these crises, or a longer-term pivot away from climate action. These get-togethers reinforce social ties among the participants. Canada: Climate hero to climate villain? At COP21 in Paris, then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau announced, “Canada is back!” The Trudeau government’s environment minister, Catherine McKenna, helped to negotiate the Paris Climate Agreement . One of Carney’s first acts as prime minister was to cancel the consumer carbon tax Trudeau brought in. And, among other things, Carney is now working to develop new oil and gas projects . At COP31, Carney was a no-show at the leaders summit. This past week, two former environment and climate change ministers criticized the record and direction of the current government. McKenna stated that the claim that Canada is still committed to its targets is “factually untrue.” Indeed, Canada consistently has one of the worst climate performance records . The Climate Change Performance Index, which compares the climate performance of 64 countries and the European Union, ranks Canada 62nd . This poor performance started before Carney’s tenure as prime minister , but Canada has been backsliding on the climate change file since he took office. In the view of many Canadians, Canada faces serious, and even existential, threats from the Trump-led United States. In the wake of this threat, Carney has been trying to boost economic growth and diversify international and domestic trade. Much of this has involved plans to grow the fossil fuel sector . The strategy has also been an attempt to assuage discontent fuelling separatist sentiments in oil-rich Alberta. What is not entirely clear is whether the direction of Carney’s energy and climate policies is a short-term strategy to deal with these crises, or a longer-term pivot away from climate action. articles.content: Prime Minister Mark Carney is riding a wave of domestic support and has emerged as the global poster child of a cautious but firm resistance to American bullies. He stood up to Donald Trump long before the recent Democratic landslide in the midterm elections in the United States. A central plank of Carney’s strategy consists of reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the U.S. by luring massive international investment to the country. Much of this investment into his “Projects of National Interest” will flow to infrastructure allowing Canada’s vast natural resources to access markets outside of North America. It would seem the midterm election results vindicate Carney. Yet, on closer inspection, things are more complicated. While Carney’s goal is commendable — a stable, sovereign Canada — the means he’s employing will arguably move Canada closer to the model of a society that is championed by … Donald Trump. Corporations benefit Consider the planned “mega tax deduction” designed to spur investment in pipelines, ports and extraction projects. The main beneficiaries would be multinational corporations and their shareholders, not Canadians. True, the investments would create jobs, but it’s worth noting that workers on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border have not received much of a share of growth in the last four decades. Other cases, such as the plan to privatize four large Canadian airports, are a classic short-term government cash grab . Compared to the Stellantis and Stelco debacles — when two major manufacturers failed to uphold job and production commitments made to Ottawa in exchange for federal backing or foreign-takeover approval — the federal government has a stronger position in the resource sector. That’s because the resources are located on Canadian soil. This opens up policy alternatives, which could include: Moving towards the Danish model of industrial foundations , where some profits are earmarked for social and environmental causes. Higher royalties from natural resource licences, which could be efficient in generating more for public coffers even if they marginally lowered private investment. Boosting the role of the Canada Infrastructure Bank to provide investment without loss of sovereignty, tied to Canada’s airports and ports. Eroding democratic norms In addition to the political substance, the Carney government’s efforts weaken democratic accountability. The omnibus Bill C-39 before Parliament weakens the rights of workers, non-governmental organizations and First Nations to contest the decisions made in the name of economic growth and “economic sovereignty.” Read more: What Bill C-39’s loosened environmental regulations could mean for Canadians Some First Nations probably feel the same way about Ottawa’s economic bulldozer strategy as Canadians feel about Trump’s actions. The Neskantaga First Nation’s battle to protect their homelands in northern Ontario is just one example. Sustainability Carney’s strategy is doubling down on the fossil fuel sector in Canada, too. This favours profit extraction and concentrated economic interests both at home and abroad over lower-income Canadians who are most likely to suffer from the consequences of climate change in terms of extreme weather, drought, wildfire and smoke. Once again, alternatives exist. Rather than export raw materials cheaply, why not invest in the processing of lumber, oil, gas, metals and minerals at home? For decades, part of Canada’s resource curse has been that most of the processing and economic value creation ( and job creation ) happens abroad, and Canadians pay dearly to purchase back the final products. Promoting forms of worker or producer co-operatives and vocational training programs would allow more evenly distributed forms of economic growth without increasing Canada’s carbon footprint. What’s more, investing in renewables has vast potential and is less prone to monopolizing profits. Read more: Fossil of the Day: Has Mark Carney made Canada a climate heretic? Carney’s amnesia? In sum, Carney’s Projects of National Interest look more like Projects of National Inequality and Environmental Destruction than measures that will promote Canada’s interests in a socially and environmentally sustainable fashion. Even without some of the more repulsive and narcissistic characteristics of Trump’s presidency, the economic policy outcome will be a country that is closer than ever before to Trump’s ideal for the U.S. The fact that someone as qualified and experienced as Carney falls into this trap is both surprising and to be expected at the same time. It’s surprising because Carney is well aware that policy measures have unintended, but foreseeable, negative consequences. In 2014, as governor of the Bank of England, he conceded that “the distributional consequences of the response to the financial crisis have been significant,” exacerbating inequality. He also founded the Network for Greening the Financial System in 2017, a group of central banks analyzing and guarding against the financial risks of climate change. In short, he sounded like a champion of sustainability. A striking case of amnesia about this former life seems to have befallen Carney since becoming prime minister. Yet it also has simple explanations. While corporate lobbyists in Ottawa may not be as powerful as they are in the U.S. capital, they clearly have substantial influence. In addition, Carney’s background as a banker predisposes him to favour financial interests over those of working Canadians when push comes to shove. What’s the point of fighting Trump when the price you pay is to import some elements of Trumpism to Canada? The consequences of Carney’s policy agenda, in terms of exacerbating the twin crises of economic inequality and environmental degradation, could be felt in Canada long after Trump has left the Oval Office.
